contents.text: The Southwest is home to many Native groups. Native people have lived in the Southwest for thousands of years. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Native people in the Southwest had to adapt to the harsh environment. Much of the Southwest is dry. Nearly half the land is covered by large deserts that receive very little rain. Tough plants that require little water, such as cactuses and dry grasses, grow well in the desert. Parts of the Southwest have extreme temperatures, with very hot days and very cold nights. During the summer, temperatures can reach over 100 degrees!

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were Native people who lived in the Southwest thousands of years ago. Read about how the Ancestral Puebloans survived in the desert. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were

farmers. This means they stayed in one place to grow crops instead of moving around to find food. Corn was one of their most important foods. It was difficult to grow crops in the desert. So the Ancestral Puebloans developed new kinds of corn that needed less water and grew well in dry areas.

textContent.text: The Ancestral Puebloans also planted corn alongside squash and beans. The squash grew close to the ground. Its leaves shaded the soil from the hot sun, which helped the ground stay moist. The corn provided a tall stalk for the beans to grow on. The beans put nutrients in the soil that helped the corn and squash grow healthy and strong.

content.text: Corn, beans, and squash growing together

pieces.text: The Zuni are another Pueblo group. Storytelling is an important Zuni tradition. A
is a shared way of life passed down from generation to generation. Read the adapted Zuni folktale. Then answer the question below.
Long ago, the world was always dark and warm. Eagle and Coyote struggled to hunt in the darkness. One morning, they walked through the desert to visit powerful spirits called
. The Katsinas had a box that held the sun and the moon. Whenever they wanted light, they opened the lid just a little.

textContent.text: Coyote and Eagle took the box while the Katsinas were sleeping. Eagle flew through the sky, carrying the box carefully. He warned Coyote not to open it, but Coyote's curiosity was too strong. He snatched the box and peeked inside.

Instantly, the sun and moon leaped out! They flew high into the sky, carrying their heat away from the earth. The sun and moon were now far from the ground. So, the air became chilly, and the wind blew more strongly for part of the year. That is why we now have winter.

Long ago, the world was always dark and warm. Eagle and Coyote struggled to hunt in the darkness. One morning, they walked through the desert to visit powerful spirits called
. The Katsinas had a box that held the sun and the moon. Whenever they wanted light, they opened the lid just a little.

contents.text: The Southwest is home to many Native groups. Native people have lived in the Southwest for thousands of years. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Native people in the Southwest had to adapt to the harsh environment. Much of the Southwest is dry. Nearly half the land is covered by large deserts that receive very little rain. During the summer, temperatures can reach over 100 degrees!

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were Native people who lived in the Southwest thousands of years ago. Read about how the Ancestral Puebloans survived in the desert. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were

farmers. This means they stayed in one place to grow crops instead of moving around to find food. Corn was one of their most important foods. It was difficult to grow crops in the desert. So the Ancestral Puebloans developed new kinds of corn that needed less water and grew well in dry areas.

textContent.text: The Ancestral Puebloans also planted corn alongside squash and beans. The squash grew close to the ground. Its leaves shaded the soil from the hot sun, which helped the ground stay moist. The corn provided a tall stalk for the beans to grow on. The beans put nutrients in the soil that helped the corn and squash grow healthy and strong.

pieces.text: The Zuni are another Pueblo group. Storytelling is an important Zuni tradition. A
is a shared way of life passed down from generation to generation. Read the adapted Zuni folktale. Then answer the question below.
Long ago, the world was always dark and warm. Eagle and Coyote struggled to hunt in the darkness. One morning, they walked through the desert to visit powerful spirits called
. The Katsinas had a box that held the sun and the moon. Whenever they wanted light, they opened the lid just a little.

textContent.text: Coyote and Eagle took the box while the Katsinas were sleeping. Eagle flew through the sky, carrying the box carefully. He warned Coyote not to open it, but Coyote's curiosity was too strong. He snatched the box and peeked inside.

Instantly, the sun and moon leaped out! They flew high into the sky, carrying their heat away from the earth. The sun and moon were now far from the ground. So, the air became chilly, and the wind blew more strongly for part of the year. That is why we now have winter.

contents.text: The Southwest is home to many Native groups. Native people have lived in the Southwest for thousands of years. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Native people in the Southwest had to adapt to the harsh environment. Much of the Southwest is dry. Nearly half the land is covered by large deserts that receive very little rain. Tough plants that require little water, such as cactuses and dry grasses, grow well in the desert. Parts of the Southwest have extreme temperatures, with very hot days and very cold nights. During the summer, temperatures can reach over 100 degrees!

contents.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were Native people who lived in the Southwest thousands of years ago. Read about how the Ancestral Puebloans survived in the desert. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: The Ancestral Puebloans were

farmers. This means they stayed in one place to grow crops instead of moving around to find food. Corn was one of their most important foods. It was difficult to grow crops in the desert. So the Ancestral Puebloans developed new kinds of corn that needed less water and grew well in dry areas.

textContent.text: The Ancestral Puebloans also planted corn alongside squash and beans. The squash grew close to the ground. Its leaves shaded the soil from the hot sun, which helped the ground stay moist. The corn provided a tall stalk for the beans to grow on. The beans put nutrients in the soil that helped the corn and squash grow healthy and strong.

pieces.text: Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest have used different methods to
, meaning change, their environment. These changes made hunting and gathering easier. Read about how Native people have modified the Pacific Northwest. Then answer the question below.
For hundreds of years, Native people have increased forest resources using intentional burning.

means carefully setting fire to certain areas. Intentional burning helps clear areas and maintain grassy prairies between forests.  Since animals like deer and elk like to eat in open areas, intentional burning makes it easier for people to hunt in grassy prairies. Burned plants also release nutrients, helping plants such as berries grow back in greater amounts.
The ocean is also a major source of food, such as fish and shellfish. Historically, coastal people built
by stacking stones to create low walls in shallow water. These walls created pools of water where clams grew well. People could harvest clams more easily in clam gardens than in the open ocean.

pieces.text: Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest have used different methods to
, meaning change, their environment. These changes made hunting and gathering easier. Read about how Native people have modified the Pacific Northwest. Then answer the question below.
For hundreds of years, Native people have increased forest resources using intentional burning.

means carefully setting fire to certain areas. Intentional burning helps clear areas and maintain grassy prairies between forests.  Since animals like deer and elk like to eat in open areas, intentional burning makes it easier for people to hunt in grassy prairies. Burned plants also release nutrients, helping plants such as berries grow back in greater amounts.
The ocean is also a major source of food, such as fish and shellfish. Historically, coastal people built
by stacking stones to create low walls in shallow water. These walls created pools of water where clams grew well. People could harvest clams more easily in clam gardens than in the open ocean.

contents.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: Native people smoked salmon so it could be stored and eaten later.

explanationText.text: The passage says that after catching salmon, people cooked it by placing it in smoke from a fire. Smoked salmon can be stored and eaten later.

content.text: Native people made different canoes for different purposes.

explanationText.text: The passage says that on rivers, Native people used small, flat-bottomed canoes designed for traveling in shallow waters. contents.text: Native groups in California made different kinds of boats depending on the materials available in their environments. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the wood inside. People used these canoes to travel and fish in rivers and along the coast.

Further south, the Chumash and Tongva groups made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into long, flat planks, then bound them together with a tar-like material and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

contents.text: Native groups in California made different kinds of boats depending on the materials available in their environments. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the wood inside. People used these canoes to travel and fish in rivers and along the coast.

Further south, the Chumash and Tongva groups made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into long, flat planks, then bound them together with a tar-like material and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

contents.text: Native groups in California made different kinds of boats depending on the materials available in their environments. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the northern forests, people made dugout canoes from enormous redwood trees. Craftsmen cut redwood trunks in half, then gently burned and carved away the wood inside. People used these canoes to travel and fish in rivers and along the coast.

Further south, the Chumash and Tongva groups made plank canoes from redwood logs. Craftsmen sawed the logs into long, flat planks, then bound them together with a tar-like material and strong string. People used these canoes for ocean fishing and trading up and down the coast.

header.text: By 1610 and 1611, the Powhatan tribes and the Jamestown settlers stopped getting along. These are some of the reasons why:

content.text: The Native Americans didn't give the settlers food during the Starving Time.

explanationText.text: The Jamestown settlers struggled to survive the Starving Time. They didn't get any food or help from the Powhatan tribes during that time. The settlers were angry that the Powhatan tribes didn't help them.

content.text: The settlers kept attacking Native Americans and stealing their land.

explanationText.text: In 1610, the Jamestown settlers killed members of the Paspahegh and Kecoughtan tribes. Also, in 1612, settlers started a new town called Henricus on the Powhatan tribes' land. The tribes tried to stop the settlers from taking more land.

header.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The Native Americans taught the settlers how to plant corn.

explanationText.text: In the past, the Powhatan tribes had helped the Jamestown settlers with their food. But by 1610, the tribes and the settlers were not getting along.

content.text: The settlers helped the Native Americans learn how to make guns.

explanationText.text: The settlers did not teach the Native Americans how to make guns. The Native Americans had their own weapons. Also, the settlers did not want to give the Native Americans new tools for attacking them.

header.text: These events show that the Powhatan tribes and the Jamestown settlers stopped getting along:

content.text: In June 1610, Jamestown settlers stole land from the Kecoughtan tribe.

explanationText.text: The Kecoughtan (kee-koh-TAN) tribe's village was right next to Jamestown. The Jamestown settlers chased the Kecoughtan off of their land. They used the Kecoughtan tribe's land for growing crops.

content.text: In August 1610, Jamestown settlers killed 50 members of the Paspahegh tribe.

explanationText.text: The Jamestown settlers killed the Paspahegh (pass-puh-HAY) queen and her children. They also killed many other members of the Paspahegh tribe.

pieces.text: This event does
show that the Powhatan tribes and settlers stopped getting along:

content.text: The Powhatan tribes brought food and supplies to the people of Jamestown.

explanationText.text: At first, the Powhatan tribes brought food to the Jamestown settlers. Bringing food showed a peaceful relationship between the Powhatan tribes and the settlers. By 1610, that peaceful relationship had ended.

header.text: By 1610 and 1611, the Powhatan tribes and the Jamestown settlers stopped getting along. These are some of the reasons why:

content.text: The settlers kept attacking Native Americans and stealing their land.

explanationText.text: In 1610, the Jamestown settlers killed members of the Paspahegh and Kecoughtan tribes. Also, in 1612, settlers started a new town called Henricus on the Powhatan tribes' land. The tribes tried to stop the settlers from taking more land.

content.text: The Native Americans didn't give the settlers food during the Starving Time.

explanationText.text: The Jamestown settlers struggled to survive the Starving Time. They didn't get any food or help from the Powhatan tribes during that time. The settlers were angry that the Powhatan tribes didn't help them.

header.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The Native Americans taught the settlers how to plant corn.

explanationText.text: In the past, the Powhatan tribes had helped the Jamestown settlers with their food. But by 1610, the tribes and the settlers were not getting along.

content.text: The settlers helped the Native Americans learn how to make guns.

explanationText.text: The settlers did not teach the Native Americans how to make guns. The Native Americans had their own weapons. Also, the settlers did not want to give the Native Americans new tools for attacking them.
